vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: nm-abstract-hook-authoring
Version: 1.0.0

The skill bundle is a comprehensive technical guide and reference for authoring lifecycle hooks in Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK. It includes detailed documentation on hook types, implementation patterns in Python and Bash, performance optimization, and security best practices such as secret redaction and input validation. While the guide describes high-risk capabilities like shell execution and tool interception, these are inherent features of the platform being documented, and the instructions are focused on 'security-first design' and defensive use cases. No malicious intent, hidden prompt injections, or unauthorized data exfiltration mechanisms were found across the files (SKILL.md, modules/*.md).

llm.summary: This is an instruction-only developer guide for writing Claude Code / SDK hooks; its requirements and examples match the stated purpose, but several example patterns (global auditing, shell-command hooks, and HTTP hook POSTs) can be misused to capture or exfiltrate sensitive data if enabled carelessly.

dimensions.detail: The name/description promise a hook-authoring security-first guide and the SKILL.md + modules contain detailed hook types, SDK callback patterns, logging, validation, performance and scope guidance—all coherent with the stated purpose.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Instructions are focused on hook implementation, validation, logging, and performance. However, many examples show writing full tool inputs/outputs to ~/.claude/audit.log, running shell commands that echo $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT, and using the HTTP hook type to POST hook payloads to arbitrary URLs—behaviors that could collect or transmit secrets if misconfigured. Some code examples also mix blocking file I/O inside async contexts (potential performance bug). These are legitimate hook patterns but carry risk if used globally or pointed at untrusted endpoints.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec and no code files to execute are provided; this is an instruction-only skill, which minimizes installer risk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required env vars or credentials. Example snippets reference environment checks (e.g., PRODUCTION_APPROVED) and runtime placeholders (CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT), which are expected for hook code. Because the examples include patterns for logging and HTTP POSTing, users should be aware these could capture secrets or environment values if not sanitized.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill itself does not request always:true or modify other skills. The guide explains global (~/.claude/settings.json) and plugin/project scopes and shows global hooks that persist across sessions; enabling such global hooks grants broad, persistent reach across all sessions and should be treated with care.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This guide is coherent and useful for building hooks, but review the examples before applying them in your environment. Key points to consider before enabling hooks from these patterns: 1) Prefer project or plugin scope during development; avoid enabling broad global hooks until reviewed. 2) Avoid logging raw tool inputs/outputs or writing them to persistent files without redaction; use the provided secret-sanitization patterns and validate them against your data formats. 3) Treat HTTP hooks as potential exfiltration channels—only POST to endpoints you control and audit network targets. 4) Sanity-check any shell-command hooks to prevent command-injection or accidental writes of secrets (don’t blindly echo $CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT to disk). 5) Test performance and ensure async file/network I/O is non-blocking (some examples mix blocking I/O inside async code). 6) Use a safe approval gating (e.g., production access checks) and vet any environment-based approvals (PRODUCTION_APPROVED). If you want extra assurance, ask the maintainer for concrete example manifests/hooks for your intended scope, or run code reviews and unit tests in a sandboxed environment before enabling globally.
